segments.text: Hi and welcome to the lecture number seven of our introduction to photonics video series.
Today's topic is going to be the light sources and we are also going to describe the anatomy of
the human eye. In general light sources can be defined as the sources that produce or emit
in the light. We have natural light sources and we also have a man-made light sources.
Man-made light sources can be further broken down into non-laser light sources
and laser light sources. This lecture is going to cover the subsection of so-called non-laser light
sources. This slide presents the list of all non-laser light sources that you may come across
in the field of photonics. So we are going to discuss so-called incandescent sources, fluorescent
or low pressure discharge lamps, high intensity and high pressure discharge lamps, flash lamps and arc
lamps, and finally light emitting diodes or popular LEDs. Popular incandescent light sources are using
tungsten as a material that the filaments are made out of. So tungsten is having a few
properties that are very interesting from the perspective of an incandescent light source
among which the most important are low vapor pressure, high melting point of 3,655 Kelvin
and finally the strength. It's also important to mention that most modern incandescent lamps
in addition to the tungsten filament are also filled with a gas with the purpose of extending
their lifetime, extending the lifetime of the filament and that gas is usually a mixture of
argon and nitrogen, although we may also come across the lamps that are based on halogen.
So halogen is used in small amounts to basically prevent the particles of tungsten
from filament to be depositing the glass. So during the process of operation of the incandescent lamp
when the tungsten is being heated to high temperatures, there's going to be particles
of tungsten that are going to be relieving the filament and deposit on the inner side of the
glass bulb. Usually this is being observed as a black coating on the inner surface of the
light bulb. In order to prevent that, we are adding special types of materials, so-called
halogen, such as bromine, chlorine and iodine that are going to prevent this type of buildup
on the inner surface of the glass of the light bulb. It's also important to mention
that halogen lamps are hot and in general all incandescent light sources are hot.
There's multiple reasons why they are kept hot, among which the most important is
need to keep the regenerating cycle going because nothing less than 500 degrees Fahrenheit
will do this regeneration. It's also important to mention that ordinary glass doesn't stand at
the high temperature that's needed for this regenerating cycle and for that reason all halogen
lamps are made of special types of heat-resistant glass or quartz. That is basically the constitutive
element of the most popular and modern types of incandescent light sources. So this slide further
describes the lamp filament. As we already mentioned, lamp filaments are made out of tungsten
wire and sometimes they are used in a straight length but very often they are formed into a coil
in order to increase the luminescence of a light bulb. So the longer the filament is, it is going
to have a better ability to produce brighter light. So that's the reason why very often the
filaments are being coiled into or formed into a coil. Sometimes we also have closed spaced coils
to secure the brighter and uniform light and sometimes we have a coil over the coil
to further increase the total length of the filament. If you are interested in a cost affordable or
less expensive types of light bulbs, they would have wide spaced filaments and these types of
filaments are very practical for many applications such as light projectors that
would not require a strong light. So as you can see from this slide, the filaments made out of
tungsten are coming in different shapes and forms that would determine the luminescence or ability
of the light bulb to produce a brighter or less bright light. The next type of light source that
we are going to mention are so-called fluorescent light sources. So these types of light sources are
not using thermal effect, they are actually using chemical effect to produce the light.
So we are talking about low pressure discharge lamps that have a fluorescent phosphor coating
on the inside of the glass and most of these fluorescent lights would consist of a mercury
discharge lamps that would emit 90% of their energy at wavelength of ultraviolet of 253.7 nanometers.
So what's basically happening in these fluorescent light sources or light bulbs is
the ultraviolet photons that are present in fluorescent bulbs would be exciting a number
of phosphors that would start producing the light and that we are seeing as a very bright
white light in the case of fluorescent bulbs. It's also important to mention that a constitutive
element of fluorescent lamps is also the electrodes, we have a cathode, hot cathode on one side
and very often sometimes cathode can also be cold and then on the other side we have anode.
It's important to mention that there's different principles on which the cold and hot electrodes
are working. So very often cold electrodes would be leading something called a rapid start
while on the other side hot cathode electrodes would give greater luminous
efficiency and because of that most lamps today use hot cathode electrodes. What we consider
so-called luminous efficiency that's a ratio of the visible light energy produced by a light source
to the electrical energy that is used as an input energy for these types of light sources.
So if you're talking about fluorescent light we are talking about 40 percent efficiency of a lamp
that's about 80 inches long and it turns out that the luminous efficiency of fluorescent lamp is
going to increase with its length so longer the fluorescent lamp is it's going to have better
efficiency and it's going to produce by the light. So on this slide on the left hand side we see a
pictorial view of the whole process that is taking place in a fluorescent light source. As we already
mentioned we have a phosphor coating on the inside of the glass and we also have a mercury
inside that's filling the glass tube. So when the electricity when the current is
brought to the two electrodes on each side on each end of the fluorescent bulb these electrons are
going to hit the mercury and mercury is going to produce ultraviolet radiation.
So these ultraviolet photons are going to be hitting the phosphorus coating on the inside
glass of the glass tube and would be exciting phosphorus and then phosphorus would start
producing bright light that we see on the outside of the of the fluorescent light.
It's also important to mention that the output of fluorescent lamp is also a function of the
ballast that is being used. We already mentioned that we have a rapid start and also we can have a
preheat ballast. Most of today's lamps operate with the rapid start balanced although the research
has suggested that the preheat balance may deal up to 20 percent higher light output as compared to
the the rapid start. A life cycle of fluorescent lamp can also be significantly affected by the
choice of the ballast. So the ballast be it either rapid start or preheat plays an important
role in the performance or function of the fluorescent light source. Next type of light
source that we are going to mention are so-called HIDs or high intensity discharge lamps. Here we
are talking about a specific type of a gas discharge lamp that is going to produce light
by means of an electric arc and plasma formation. So electric arc is going to be formed between the
tungsten electrodes that are housed inside of the of the glass bulb made out of either fused quartz
or fused alumina. The tube is filled with both gas and metal salts where gas facilitates the initial
strike of the arc and once we have an arc started what's going to happen is that the temperature is
going to rise and the metal salts inside of the glass tube are going to start evaporating and
forming plasma and the plasma formation in turn is going to increase the intensity of light that's
being produced by the arc between the electrodes. As already mentioned fused quartz or fused
alumina arc tubes are filled with different types of metal halides or mercury and sodium
and they're under the pressure that's why they are called high intensity high pressure
discharge lamps so the pressure is about two to four atmospheres and it's also important to
mention that very often these lamps are going to have two glass envelopes the inner quartz
discharge tube and an outer glass jacket. The outer glass jacket has a main purpose of absorption
of ultraviolet radiation that's being produced or generated by the internal operation of the bulb.
In certain instances the outer jacket can be broken through certain external effect
and in such a case if the outer jacket is broken a substantial levels of the ultraviolet
radiation are going to be emitted outside of the bulb which poses certain risk for
skin burn and eye inflammation from from this radiation so it's important for that to be
addressed in certain way it turns out that the lamp that would that these types of lamps would
automatically extinguish if the outer envelope is broken or punctured so that reduces the risk of
of a skin burn or eye inflammation due to this dangerous UV radiation that can be getting out of
these bulbs the outer jacket is broken. This slide presents a few pieces of information about
flash lamps and arc lamps. Here we are still talking about high intensity discharge devices
that are commonly used in photography and laser technology so we are talking about slightly
smaller types of light sources. They also contain certain types of gases and their operation is also
based on a flash or arc that's initiated by the high voltage across the discharge tube.
So what's going to happen inside is the ionization of the gas and production of the high intensity
light with output peaks in both the visible and infrared regions of the electromagnetic spectrum.
If you are looking at the size of these so-called quartz tubes it's usually about 1.5 millimeter in
thickness with the metal electrode at each end. There's also certain cases where water jackets
are provided for cooling purposes of these types of lamps. And finally we are going to mention our
good friend LED or light emitting a diode. Here we are talking about a semiconductor device
that is emitting a light based on a certain different effect compared to the light sources
that we already mentioned. Most of LED devices are made of aluminum gallium arsenide and they are
very common in fiber optic communications, packet calculators and other visual displays.
We are very familiar with semic segment displays that are also used in electronics.
So these devices can emit light in both the visible and infrared regions of the spectrum
based on the application. And there's certain differences between laser diodes and
LED diodes that we are going to elaborate more in the classes that follow. So in the case of an
LED or light emitting diode, light is emitted in all directions and it's based on so-called
spontaneous emission as opposed to the to the laser, semiconductor laser diodes where
above certain threshold so-called stimulated emission is taking place. So it's also important
to elaborate that the power from LEDs is generally in the microwatt range up to maybe a few milliwatts
so the power is not that high but there's a whole bunch of other advantages especially their size
and their cost. So again LEDs are small in size, they are low temperature type of devices,
they are rugged and they are relatively inexpensive. So not only that they use in electronics today
we also have regular household types of light bulbs that are based on LED technology. They are
slightly more expensive than regular traditional incandescent bulbs but they are also much more
efficient than traditional incandescent bulbs. So in order to fully understand the operation of
an LED you should have a little bit of a background in electronic devices, specifically
the basics of semiconductor-based pn junctions. So here we are talking about semiconductor
most of the time silicon that's being doped with n-type of material on one side
and a p-type of material on the other side. So one side of the so-called n-type of silicon
has excess of electrons while the other side has an excess of the holes or positive charges and then
there's also the boundary or the barrier between the two that is three of any kind of electrons
or holes and presents the barrier to the free flow of the current. This barrier can either shrink
or expand based on how the diode is biased with an external source. So in the case of a forward
bias this barrier between the p and n junction is going to shrink and is going to enable
the current carriers to jump from one side to the other and establish the current.
And in the case of the reverse bias this barrier is going to expand and it's going to
further prevent any kind of current through this barrier. In other words, in such a case,
in the case of reverse bias, the pn junction or the diode is going to be blocking any kind of
flow of the current. What is of interest for us when we are talking about light emitting diodes,
which is just a special type of a diode, is that in the case of a forward bias
when the barrier between the p and n type of a silicon is reduced to the minimum,
the current carriers are going to be moving from one side to the other.
And it turns out that as the current carriers or electrons are moving from one side to the other,
they are going to be moving from the higher energy state to a lower energy state.
And in order to meet the law of conservation of the energy, these electrons will be releasing
the energy in the form of photons, which is basically the light that we are observing on
a macroscopic scale in the case of an LED. So that's in a nutshell how a light emitting
diode works. So it's important to understand the basic theory behind the operation of the
regular diode that's based on a pn junction on a specific type of semiconductor.
The next subject that we are going to study is the anatomy of a human eye.
This is an important subject from the perspective of the safety that has to be
implemented in a photonics lab. It turns out that certain light sources of a laser type are
posing a certain hazard, a safety hazard to sensitive parts of our body, especially to the
human eye and also to the skin. So in order to really understand the whole background behind
this laser safety hazard, we have to understand the anatomy of the human eye.
So a human eye represents a complex optical system that's designed to receive focus and detect light.
We are talking about a human organ that is roughly of the shape of a slightly elongated sphere
about the size of a quarter of an inch of diameter. The outer white layer of the eye,
so-called sclera, sclera has a certain internal fluids, specifically so-called vitreous humor and
actuous humor that helps maintain the shape of the eye. The light is going to pass through the
front portion of the eye, that so-called cornea, into the eye. And then once the light enters the
eye, it's going to be passing through the lens that is going to be focusing all the light
onto the small spot in the back of the eye, which is so-called the retina. So that's exactly
why the certain light sources are dangerous to the eye, because the huge amounts of light that
are entering through the front portion of the eye are going to be focused on the smallest part.
So the irradiance, the concept of the power over the area that we introduced
in one of the previous lectures is going to increase significantly. So again, all the power
that's entering through the pupil, through the front portion of the eye, is going to be
focused on a small spot. So we are reducing the area, and in turn, we are increasing the
irradiance of that light that's reaching the back of the eye. And that's what poses the safety hazard.
So when the light reaches the back of the eye, it is going to hit the optical nerve,
and the cells of the optical nerve are going to relay that optical image in the
form of electrical signals to the brain for interpretation. We already mentioned the
irradiance, which is a power over the area. It turns out that the light irradiance on the retina
is 100,000 times greater than the light irradiance at the front of the eye due to the focusing
ability of the lens that's a part of the eye. So here we're talking about considerable optical gain
that can create eye hazard when stray laser beams are entering the eye. A little bit more
information about the anatomy of the human eye, specifically a little bit about the cornea and
so-called aqueous humor. So when we're talking about the cornea, we're talking about the
outermost transparent layer that covers the front of the eye. This part of the eye can withstand
dust, sand, and other assaults from the environment. And the reason for that is because the cells of
the cornea have ability to regenerate themselves or to replace themselves within 40 or 48 hours. So
even mild injuries to the cornea are healed quickly. The aqueous humor is a liquid,
mostly water, between the cornea and the lens. This water in the aqueous humor absorbs the
heat and protects the internal portion of the eye from any kind of thermal radiation. It turns out
that index of refraction of this part of the human eye is approximately 1.33, which is exactly
the index of refraction of the water. We already mentioned the lens, which is a focusing mechanism
in the eye. So we are talking about the flexible tissue that changes shape in the conjunction
cornea. The lens will be focusing light on the back of the eye, and it has this ability
to change the shape. And if it's changing shape, the focal length of this lens is going to change,
which would enable the eye to focus on both near and far objects. We also have iris that controls
the amount of light that enters the eye. That's going to be the pigmented or colored part of the
eye that responds to the light intensity by adjusting its size. So if we are in a light
environment, the pupil, which is the dark spot at the center of the iris, is going to reduce its
size. And by doing that, naturally, it's going to prevent a huge amount of light from entering
the eye. On the other side, if we are in a dark environment, the pupil is going to open or it's
going to dilate, and it's going to enable the maximum of the light to enter the eye.
So as far as the pupil is concerned, again, we are talking about opening the center of the iris.
The size of the pupil is changing from two to seven millimeters. We are talking about the
dilation of the pupil. And as already mentioned, dark in the environment, the larger the pupil,
fully dilated pupil that's expanded to admit the greatest amount of light is about seven
millimeters. We also have a so-called vitreous humor that is a colorless gel that fills the
large area at the center of the eyeball. And it's main purpose is to help and maintain the
shape of the eye. One of the most important parts of the human eye is so-called retina.
Retina is located in the back of the eye, and it is a light sensitive layer that can be viewed as
a small screen onto which all the light is being focused through the cornea and the lens. Retina
is directly connected to the optical nerve. So all the excitation from the light that's coming
to the eye is going to be turned into the electrical pulses that are collected on the retina and
further transferred to the optical nerve. The retina contains two types of photo-receptors,
so-called rods and cones that are operating differently in different environments,
either light or dark. It's often important to mention that signals that are transmitted
through the optical nerve are going all the way to the brain, and that's how we are developing
the sense of vision. We also have a fovea that represents the most sensitive central part of the
retina, and that is the area that's responsible for the most detailed vision that each human being
has. Foveal lesion caused by the laser radiation is a worst case scenario for vision, and that's
exactly why we have the potential hazard when we are operating with the lasers, especially high
power lasers. It's also important to mention that sensitivity of the human eye to the light
is not the same for all the wavelengths. For example, it turns out that the ultraviolet range
of light that ranges from 315 to 280 nanometers or 280 to 100 nanometers, which is ultraviolet B
and finally ultraviolet C, are primarily absorbed in the cornea in the front portion of the eye.
And for that reason UV light in most cases is not as dangerous as other wavelengths of light.
If we are looking at the range of 315 to 400 nanometers, which we are still in an ultraviolet
range, these wavelengths are going to be absorbed principally in the lens of the eye, so they are
also not being transferred to the lens all the way to the back of the retina. The most hazardous
is going to be the infrared radiation, especially infrared A range, and the reason for that is that
the infrared radiation is passing to both the cornea and lens and finally reaches the retina,
which is in the back of the eye. So the whole absorption of this type of light radiation is in
a retinal pigment, which is the dark brown layer with exceptionally large blood vessels and high
blood flow rate, which represents the most sensitive part of the retina, and that's the
reason why these wavelengths are the most hazardous for the human eye. And finally, we also want to
mention the safety hazard to a different human organ, which is our skin. So there's a certain
potential risk to the skin, however these are considered secondary to the risks to the eyes.
So skin injuries due to laser exposure may affect only the external dead layer of the skin cells.
This impact can be either thermal or photochemical. In order to fully understand
the impact of the laser light to the skin, we also have to understand the anatomy of the skin.
When we are talking about skin, we are talking about two main layers, so-called epidermis,
which is the surface layer, and the dermis, which is underlying layer. So this outer layer also has
its surface, the so-called stratum corneum, that consists mainly of the dead cells
and gives protection against the water loss, abrasion, dust, air, and other environmental
effects. If you're looking at a layer of epidermis that's just below the stratum corneum,
there we have specialized cells that produce the melanin pigment granules, and that is responsible
for the darkest of our skin, and that type of melanin pigment is actually responsible for
the protection of our skin against harmful ultraviolet radiation. So these cells are
absorbing the radiation, they darken, and they're responsible for the skin color change
during the sun tanning. As we already mentioned, the laser light can also be a safety hazard for
the skin. It turns out that the skin reflects most of the visible and infrared radiation,
while the absorption happens in an ultraviolet range. For that reason, especially for the
ultraviolet A and ultraviolet B range, the skin is very sensitive, so these types of radiations
can be harmful from the perspective of their absorption in a human skin. So with enough
power and duration, the instant radiation of any wavelength can penetrate the protective filters
and layers of the epidermis and cause deep internal injuries. So again, important to
mention that ultraviolet is the most critical, but we don't want to restrict potential hazards
to the ultraviolet only because other wavelengths can also pose a safety risk if they reach certain
powers and certain durations of exposure. Laser-induced thermal change to the skin
is most pronounced in a far infrared wavelength, such as those produced by CO2 lasers, so
certain types of lasers are also a safety risk for our skin in addition to the safety hazards
to our eyes. With this, we are going to conclude our lecture number seven. So in this lecture,
we elaborated on light sources. We mentioned at the beginning of this course that photonics deals
with all aspects of the light, including the light production, so we are going to need light sources
in our photonics labs, in our photonics experiments, because in order to create the optical system and
in order to manipulate with the light and put it to proper use, we need to first produce the
light, and for that purpose, we are going to be using the light sources that are elaborated to
certain extent in this lecture. So we covered non-laser man-made types of light sources.
We are going to be talking about other light sources, especially laser types in the lectures
that follow in different courses. And then finally, in this lecture, we also elaborated on the
anatomy of the human eye and the skin from the perspective of the safety hazards that
exist in photonics labs when we are operating with different types of light sources.
So next time, in lecture number eight, now that we know about anatomy of the human eye and the
skin, we are going to talk about important aspects of the laser safety and how it is to be
implemented in the photonics lab, so that everyone is safe and no risk to the safety of
our eyes and our skin is increased or present in the lab. With this, we are going to conclude
lecture number seven here, and I wish you the nice rest of the day, and I'll see you next time in
lecture eight.
